To extend these efficiency gains across servers, we also design a secure sharding mechanism that distributes client requests. We demonstrate that strong privacy guarantees can coexist with efficient authentication at scale; STAR processes authentication requests in tens of microseconds and handles approximately 13.9K requests per second per CPU core.
items.title: STAR: Scalable TEE-based Anonymous Rate-limiter

items.summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly acting through Web interfaces and external tools. They produce trajectories. Those trajectories may pass through several intermediaries. They can store, modify, or dispute those trajectories. In Web-based agent deployments, trajectories may pass through APIs, marketplaces, and tool servers. As such, a copied or disputed log may not by itself reveal which agent owner produced it. Behavioral watermarking can embed ownership evidence in agent action choices. However, existing methods mainly address detection, removal, rewriting, or imitation. They do not directly test whether repeated observation of watermarked trajectories enables cross-session forgery by exploiting learned action preferences. We formulate this learned-forgery threat and propose AgentAnchor, a session-keyed behavioral watermark for owner attribution from trajectory logs. We derive each step key from a secret key, a fresh public session identifier, and semantic states of recent observations, while a guarded digest of the action-policy state diversifies linear coding rows. It embeds parity evidence through a KL-bounded exponential tilt, and a trusted verifier checks a disputed log without rerunning the agent, using wrong-key calibration and abstention.
items.title: Session-Bound Behavioral Watermarking for Autonomous LLM Agents

items.summary: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) traffic-signal controllers may use vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I) reports, exposing their perception layer to false-data injection. Existing demonstrations typically assume either white-box access to the controller's weights or full observability of the traffic state. We study the impact of a weaker and more realistic adversary who has no access to the RL model and whose traffic observations are limited to her own approach. This black-box, minimally informed attacker trains an imitation surrogate of the controller. She then crafts bounded fake reports, restricted to inflating vehicle counts on her own approach, that transfer to the real controller. We demonstrate that despite the loss of accuracy relative to an attacker who can observe the entire state and action space, this limited attacker can significantly increase the average waiting time for other approaches while barely changing the waiting time on her own approach, i.e. externalizing the added delay onto the other approaches. Because the only realizable move is to inflate one's own reported queue, we find that a zero-knowledge attacker that simply reports the maximum feasible queue is as damaging as the surrogate-based one, while an unstructured random inflation is not: the surrogate is not required to reproduce the degradation, and the exposed vulnerability is the V2I sensing channel itself. The surrogate's role is directional control, selecting a disruptive or a selfish objective at the same budget. The attack persists under +/-20% uniform demand variation. Finally, on a common per-lane budget we place the attacker on a knowledge ladder against white-box adversaries, and find the black-box surrogate matches a realizable white-box attacker that uses the victim's own gradients; only abandoning realizability raises the damage further.
items.title: A Minimally Informed Black-Box Fake-Report Attack on DRL Traffic-Signal Control

items.summary: Organisations frequently utilise Privacy Impact Assessments (PIAs), Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs), or even Fundamental Rights Impact Assessments (FRIAs) to identify and evaluate potential risks and possible infringements of fundamental rights. While the adoption of PIAs and DPIAs has grown significantly in recent years, robust scientific evidence regarding their operational challenges, implementation strategies, and tangible benefits remains scarce. In particular, empirical research conducted post-enactment of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is notably limited -- especially studies that directly interview professionals about their PIA/DPIA practices or their engagement with FRIAs. To do so, in this paper we leveraged semi-structured interviews to elicit privacy professionals' perspectives on PIA/DPIA activities and analysed the responses using reflexive thematic analysis. As a result, this work provides a comprehensive thematic framework for the field, offering a rich and thick description of professionals' views and experiences. In total, 26 participants from 17 countries were interviewed, revealing how they plan and conduct PIAs/DPIAs, including how they assess trade-offs, the benefits and challenges they perceive, and how they view the interplay between PIAs/DPIAs and the EU AI Act. Among the main findings were low adherence to established DPIA methodologies; differences and similarities between PIAs and DPIAs; a perceived neglect of data subjects' interests during DPIA processes; discussions on building FRIAs on top of DPIAs; and the potential for holistic impact assessments, though accompanied by concerns regarding assessment fatigue. Thus, this study informs privacy professionals about real-world challenges and experiences of PIA/DPIA implementation, and guides researchers toward future research directions.
items.title: The State of the Practice in Privacy Impact Assessments: Understanding the Professionals' Perspectives, Experiences, and Current Procedures

items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled more effective vulnerability scanning of web applications. However, these capabilities also make it significantly easier for attackers to automate cyberattacks on the web. In this work, we investigate how to divert malicious LLM-based web scanning, with preservation of genuine functionality as a deployment requirement. We systematically study six LLM-based scanners and summarize how they gather information and iteratively select actions based on observations. Guided by the study, we then present WebMaze, a defense that preserves genuine application functionality while diverting LLM-based scanners to a generated decoy world. WebMaze embeds functionality-coupled traps in genuine pages and constructs view-tailored interactive decoy worlds from the application's existing views. The traps blend into genuine components and expose entry points to decoy worlds that sustain exploration through connected pages and interactions without changing genuine functionality. Across 12 web applications and three LLM-based scanners under the default no-disclosure setting, decoy pages account for an average of 93.0% of the distinct pages requested per run. This demonstrates that WebMaze effectively diverts scanners away from genuine application pages and into the generated decoy worlds. Even when explicitly informed about the decoy mechanism and instructed to avoid decoy pages, scanners continue to explore predominantly decoy pages.
items.title: WebMaze: Defending Against LLM-Powered Web Scanners with Functionality-Coupled Deception

items.summary: Coding agents automatically load project memory files such as CLAUDE.md at the start of every session and treat them as trusted project guidance. Anyone who can change such a file, for example through a pull request, can therefore steer the agent without ever touching the developer's prompt. We study memory files as an attack surface for insecure code generation and ask (1) whether a malicious memory file makes agents produce code that passes its tests but is vulnerable, and (2) whether agents disclose to the developer that the file shaped their code. For each of 12 CWE classes, we crafted two malicious memory files, a qualified variant that presents removing defensive checks as engineering best practice and a forceful variant that demands it. We ran Claude Code (Sonnet 5.5) and OpenCode (Qwen 3.8 27B, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) on 36 SecRepoBench tasks with and without these files. The malicious files changed the rate of secure completions by -8 to +6 percentage points, with no consistent pattern across agents or variants. Agents differ sharply in what they tell the developer about the file. Claude Code names it in about two thirds of its final messages, whereas OpenCode mentions it almost exclusively in its reasoning trace, not in the final message the developer reads. Flagging the file as an attack does not reliably protect the code, as such agents still generated vulnerable code. We outline the larger studies needed to quantify this risk across agents and to design defenses.
items.title: Security Impact of Coding Agent's Memory Files

items.summary: Register-Transfer Level (RTL) simulators are fundamental to modern IC design workflows, yet like any complex software, they frequently contain critical bugs that compromise simulation accuracy. To systematically stress-test these tools, we introduce GI-RTL-Fuzz, a grammar-informed fuzzing framework that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate high-quality RTL test cases. Our key innovation is guiding the LLM's generation process using Backus-Naur Form (BNF) grammar coverage information, enabling the exploration of complex and rarely-tested language features. By performing differential testing against different RTL simulators, our framework uncovered a significant number of previously unknown inconsistencies in both the linting process and simulation results of major Verilog simulators.
items.title: GI-RTL-Fuzz: Grammar-Informed RTL Generation with LLMs for End-to-End Differential Simulator Fuzzing

items.summary: As the advent of large-scale quantum computing threatens classical encryption, Quasi-Cyclic Moderate Density Parity-Check (QC-MDPC) codes have emerged as a foundational element of Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC). However, decoding these relatively dense codes using classical Belief Propagation algorithms often leads to failures caused by short graph cycles that stall the decoder. In cryptographic applications, these failures are severe security vulnerabilities that leak secret key information. To address this, this paper proposes a Recurrent Bipartite Graph Neural Network (R-BGNN) as proof of concept. By integrating Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) into the message-passing framework and employing a multi-topology curriculum training strategy, the R-BGNN actively learns to break limit-cycle oscillations. Evaluated across 20 unseen matrix topologies, the proposed architecture significantly outperforms classical Bit-Flipping and Min-Sum baselines, reducing the Decoding Failure Rate (DFR) by 63.7\% at moderate noise levels ($t=10$) while converging in fewer iterations.
items.title: Recurrent Bipartite Graph Neural Networks for QC-MDPC Error Decoding in McEliece Cryptosystems

items.summary: AI agents now install packages, call model APIs with their operators' keys and change code in repositories that deploy to production. The network, credentials and write access they need are also how they can leak data, steal a key or change a system nobody approved. Sandboxes contain an agent but leave little evidence of what crossed their boundary; tracing records what happened but contains nothing. We present Tracekit Box, an open-source system (MIT, v0) that does both. Each job runs in its own Firecracker micro-VM with no network card. The only ways out are doors on the host, served over vsock: commands, outbound connections, secrets, model calls and the workspace patch. At every door a Tracekit signer the agent cannot reach decides what passes and signs it into one run per box. Names are resolved on the host; private and cloud-metadata addresses are always refused; secrets never enter the VM, which sees placeholders the host proxy swaps for real values only in one header for bound hosts; and changes come back as a patch applied file by file after the signer decides each file. Box fails closed, and each job ends as a .tkb bundle anyone can verify offline. All 13 end-to-end checks pass on a real KVM runner (the test that runs them takes 28.5 s, including image pull and boot); 15 fuzz targets on the trust boundary produced nine findings, all fixed; and the demo run's 102 signed records verify. Box does not yet run Firecracker's jailer, needs a co-located signer, and records processes inside the VM only where they cross a door.
items.title: Tracekit Box: Running AI Agents in Micro-VMs Where Every Way Out Is Decided and Signed

items.summary: Machine unlearning aims to reproduce the behavior of a model trained without designated data. For probabilistic decision models, this target also depends on the candidate options supplied at inference. We introduce DecisionUnlearn-Bench, an empirical framework that compares full, unlearned, and retain-only models across deletion granularities, label renderings, and candidate sets. Across 20 eligible model configurations on the BANKING77 dataset, full-to-oracle displacement increases consistently from example to association to class deletion. Replacing semantic option labels with opaque codes nearly eliminates the retrained oracle's recognition of deleted classes, even with successful acquisition of the full model, whereas changing the candidate set alters both the oracle and the measured unlearning progress. SimNPO satisfies the screening criterion in 19 of 20 configurations, but its gains vary substantially across seeds and deletion targets. Development tuning on the CLINC150 dataset does not establish a positive pooled effect across 48 intents. At approximately matched suppression, methods can differ markedly in oracle fidelity. Recovery experiments further distinguish initial forgetting from subsequent adaptation and show conclusions that depend on both architecture and metric. These results show that evaluating decision-model unlearning relative to a schema-specific retraining target, with separate reporting of effect size, utility, robustness, and recoverability.
items.title: DecisionUnlearn-Bench: Unlearning Probabilistic Decisions under Changing Schemas

items.summary: The external sources retained in our non-systematic audit did not isolate the incremental security or utility effect of consuming /llms.txt while ordinary retrieval remained fixed. The initial audit covered 39 sources through August 16, 2026, with later targeted updates through October 14. A purposive 15-tool study observed no automatic requests in 45 trials at one endpoint; a non-probability log study found that 97% of domains with detected files received no recorded requests in May 2026. We separate publication, fetch, model use, and action; define five operational threat paths and paired security-utility estimands; and exercise deterministic pre-model controls with 30 author-defined parser fixtures. We also execute a reduced pilot: 24 tasks across eight sites, five conditions, and 120 real model responses, with ordinary evidence held fixed. Frozen automatic scoring identifies attacker-target adoption in $21/24$ raw adversarial responses, with one further response unresolved; the adversarial URLs-only condition has no known adoptions and one unresolved response. The pilot measures output changes conditional on supplied evidence, without live retrieval or external actions. Together, the framework and pilot distinguish manifest-content effects from publication, discovery, and downstream execution, while leaving full retrieval and agent evaluation open.
items.title: Manifest-Assisted Retrieval in Artificial Intelligence Search: Evidence Gaps and a Security Evaluation

items.summary: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) enables computation on encrypted data and is promising for privacy-preserving computing. However, FHE deployment remains constrained due to massive computational, memory, and data-movement overheads. Existing acceleration strategies often overlook the storage I/O bottleneck caused by the enormous size of FHE data in large-scale applications, as most prior works focus on small benchmarks that fit in main memory. Our studies show that state-of-the-art FHE systems spend 71\% to 85\% of their execution time moving data between storage and compute units rather than performing useful computation. To address the I/O bottleneck, we present Rosemary, a heterogeneous FHE acceleration system that incorporates a novel in-storage processing (ISP) architecture with compiler-level and algorithmic optimizations. Our key innovations include 1) an adaptable hardware-aware FHE engine inside a NAND flash-based solid-state drive (SSD) for efficient and cost-effective in-storage FHE processing, 2) a Throughput-Data-Aware Program Allocator (TDAP) that partitions FHE workloads into heterogeneous programs, and 3) a Compiler-Level Ciphertext-Aware Optimizer (CLCAO) that exploits ISP-friendly FHE kernels for low-cost ISP execution. Across a diverse set of FHE workloads, including encrypted deep learning inference and cloud database queries, Rosemary achieves geometric-mean speedups of $185.7\times$ over state-of-the-art CPU/GPU implementations and $3.7\times$ over prior FHE accelerators, while improving energy efficiency by up to $3.9\times$ and Energy-Delay-Area-Product (EDAP) by up to $16.5\times$.
items.title: Rosemary: Efficient and Adaptable In-Storage Acceleration for Fully Homomorphic Encryption

items.summary: LLM-based agents now share experiences on social platforms and remember new preferences to enhance their performance. However, existing memory systems contain a vulnerability in role-to-principal attribution that attackers can exploit. We identify Role Grounding Misattribution, in which an attacker-designed interaction causes the victim agent to incorrectly record a preference from the attacker as a preference of the victim's user. Specifically, we are the first to formalize Role Grounding Attack (RGA), an attack model that exploits this vulnerability through nested conversation structures. In the memory formation stage, an experience-sharing post quoting a conversation between the attacker agent and its user is published, which explicitly identifies its publisher. The inner conversation expresses preferences from the user of the attacker agent. When the victim agent remembers preferences from this nested structure, its memory loses the context binding and grounds the attacker's preference to the victim's user instead. In the memory retrieval stage, the misattributed preference persists and influences the victim agent's decisions when it encounters relevant scenarios. We instantiate RGA as tool selection manipulation and privacy leakage. Tool selection manipulation causes a tool-call preference to be misattributed to the victim's user, steering the victim toward an attacker-controlled tool. Privacy leakage extends this by misattributing both a tool-call preference and a task-requirement preference to the victim's user. The victim selects the attacker's tool, then includes sensitive information in tool arguments to satisfy the task requirement. We evaluate RGA across five mainstream memory systems and six language models. Tool manipulation and privacy leakage both achieve high attack success rates. These results call for stronger role grounding.
items.title: Is it my preference? Role Grounding Attack against Agent's Memory via Social Interaction

items.summary: Whole-prompt translation evaluates a request in different languages but does not compare which component carries a language. We introduce a paired reversal: translate the complete request component or the complete operation component into the same target language, holding behaviour, English frame and translated-span count fixed. Component identity and non-English text quantity change together. Assigning English, Chinese and Spanish independently to the two components yields nine configurations on 190 of 300 sampled harmful behaviours retained after consensus annotation and automatic gating. Refusal scored by language-model judges is the primary outcome; unsafe compliance is reported separately. On Gemini 2.5 Flash and DeepSeek, three refusal swaps are about 5.3 percentage points and the fourth is -0.5; none survives the pre-specified six-test Holm correction. In an exploratory extension, Mistral Small 4 has a 13.7-point Spanish swap (95% interval [8.4, 18.9]), which survives the twelve-test Holm sensitivity correction under the primary judge, and 12.1 points under a second judge. GPT-5.4-mini estimates are within 2 points of zero. Component assignment supplies an additional evaluation dimension. Evaluations should record component languages and translated text quantity, comparing matched behaviours at equal translated-span count while interpreting refusal and unsafe compliance separately.
items.title: Component Translation and Judge-Labelled Refusal: A Multilingual Safety Evaluation

items.summary: Modern enterprises increasingly operate through complex information systems (IS) enabled by cloud computing, remote and hybrid work practices, and digitally integrated supply chains. These structural shifts have expanded organizational attack surfaces and weakened traditional perimeter-based trust assumptions, giving rise to new and persistent forms of cyber threats. In response, adversaries have shifted toward identity-centric, trust-based intrusion techniques that exploit legitimate access within organizational systems. This evolution has created a pronounced speed asymmetry, whereby attackers can adapt and act at machine speed while defenders remain constrained by reactive or rule-based incident response (IR) processes. Drawing on design science research, we propose ZT-AIR, an adaptive IR artifact that uses zero trust architecture as its design theory and hierarchical reinforcement learning as its kernel theory. ZT-AIR learns context-aware trust decisions, separates strategic prioritization from tactical execution, encodes zero-trust controls as actions, and jointly optimizes security effectiveness and operational continuity. Experimental results across diverse adversarial strategies, network scales, and defense environments show that ZT-AIR achieves a strong balance between security and continuity through frequent, minimally disruptive interventions. Practitioner validation further confirms the design's practical viability. This study contributes to IS research by extending computational design science from threat identification to response execution, theorizing zero trust architecture for adaptive IR, and deriving reusable design principles for adaptive decision support artifacts.
items.title: Zero Trust-Enabled Adaptive Incident Response using Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning

items.summary: Web assistants increasingly answer questions about a user's private documents by pairing a small on-device model with a cloud LLM behind a Web API. In collaborative decoding, the document stays on the client, and the cloud receives only a public view that the user approves, such as the question alone, but the two models exchange messages while the answer is generated. We show that the message transcript can disclose private content that neither the public view nor the answer contains. In a planted-secret audit, speculative decoding with private drafts did not include the secret code in its answers, yet sent the code to the cloud in rejected drafts. We present ADLER, a decoding protocol for streaming LLM APIs in which every message to the cloud depends only on the public view and the answer the user sees, regardless of how the client combines the two models or how the cloud behaves. A client-side leakage ledger then bounds how much the answer itself reveals relative to a public reference process built from the cloud's replies. In the audit, no ADLER configuration exposed the secret beyond the answer. On GSM8K math problems with numerical values masked in the cloud's input, ADLER with an unlimited leakage budget raises the exact-match accuracy of a 0.5B client from 0.41 to 0.83 and of a 1.5B client from 0.67 to 0.85 under lenient answer parsing, close to the 0.92 achieved by uploading the full problem. It also exceeds a zero-leakage program baseline (0.69) by 0.14 and 0.16, respectively. In this baseline, the cloud writes a program that the client runs offline using the private numbers. The ledger records the disclosure charge associated with this gain; budgets of 16 nats or less leave accuracy near the cloud-only baseline on GSM8K.
items.title: Answer-Only Disclosure: Private-Context LLM Assistance over Web APIs with a Leakage Ledger

items.summary: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are widely deployed in safety- and privacy-critical domains such as healthcare and finance, where models are trained on confidential data. This paper presents the first hardware-level attribute-stealing attack that bypasses state-of-the-art privacy defenses, revealing that accelerator optimizations intended for performance can directly undermine data confidentiality. SparseBleed requires no access to gradients, logits, model weights, ground-truth labels, power traces, DVFS manipulation, shared caches, or other channels. Instead, we show that sparsity-driven execution paths encode stable timing signatures that act as a surrogate for model confidence, enabling high-fidelity attribute inference from a single query. SparseBleed generalizes across heterogeneous backends and hardware engines, including Intel AVX2/AVX-512/AMX, NVIDIA Ampere Tensor Cores with 2:4 sparsity, and nine well-known sparse and dense libraries such as Intel oneDNN, oneMKL SparseBLAS, and NVIDIA cuSPARSE. We evaluate SparseBleed to infer sensitive input attributes and true output labels. On Texas-100X, SparseBleed infers sensitive input attributes such as Sex with 66.39% accuracy and recovers the true output label, Surgical Procedure, with 99.8% accuracy. Finally, we evaluate mitigations. Constant-time execution by disabling sparsity optimizations is expensive (e.g., up to $2\times$ higher latency on NVIDIA Sparse Tensor Cores and $\approx 25\%$ higher power in AMX microbenchmarks). By contrast, a padding defense that equalizes responses to the worst-case time masks timing leakage with only 7.24% average performance overhead across nine libraries on Texas-100X/Adult and near-zero extra energy.
items.title: SPARSEBLEED: Bypassing Attribute-Inference Defenses via Sparsity Optimizations

items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are vulnerable to visual jailbreak attacks that bypass safety safeguards. Existing methods typically optimize isolated adversarial examples, limiting attack diversity, transferability, and generalization. We propose Jailbreak Connectivity (JC), a framework based on the observation that effective adversarial inputs can be connected through low-loss regions in image space. JC optimizes continuous adversarial paths: path sampling yields diverse jailbreak images, lightweight surrogate classifiers guide cross-model transfer, and a distribution-level objective enables universal attacks across harmful queries. On MM-SafetyBench, JC achieves average attack success rates of 84.01%, 85.77%, and 97.95% on Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, InternVL3.5-8B, and Gemma-3-12B-IT, respectively, exceeding the strongest baselines by up to 68.36 percentage points. In black-box evaluations, JC improves attack success rates over FigStep by 24.69 and 27.34 percentage points on GPT-5.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro, respectively. These findings reveal structured vulnerabilities in MLLM safety alignment and inform more comprehensive security evaluation.
items.title: Jailbreak Connectivity: Towards Diverse, Transferable, and Universal Multimodal Large Language Model Jailbreak

items.summary: Physical-layer fingerprinting (PLF) has emerged as a promising authentication approach for Internet of Things devices. However, most PLF systems acquire and process a fixed-length waveform for every authentication query, burdening resource-constrained edge nodes. To address this issue, we propose a progressive-observation PLF method that adapts the waveform length to each query. Specifically, a lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN) first rejects clearly unknown devices from a short observation. Spectral matching then accepts clearly registered devices from a slightly longer observation. Only ambiguous queries proceed to the same matching on the full-length waveform, reducing both data acquisition and computation. Because fingerprints drift across days, we also design an adaptive calibration algorithm to avoid retraining the CNN. The algorithm realigns the features and decision thresholds using a few current-day references from registered devices. We evaluate the method with 100BASE-TX Ethernet devices of two controller types on held-out days. Compared with fixed-length processing, it keeps the false rejection and false acceptance rates equal or lower for both controller types on both days. It also reduces the waveform data per query by 75.1% and the CPU processing time on a Raspberry Pi 5 by 73.7% on average. With the same monitoring bandwidth, an edge node can therefore serve about four times as many authentication queries.
items.title: Progressive-Observation Physical-Layer Fingerprinting for Efficient Open-Set Ethernet Authentication

items.summary: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) standards establish algorithms for quantum-safe systems, but empirical evidence about how software projects implement and maintain PQC support remains limited. We investigate this implementation and maintenance work by mining 114,361 commits and 5,713 issues across 179 open-source repositories. We use human annotation and validated LLM classification to identify PQC algorithms in commits, classify their adoption status and deployment mode, and identify technical challenges in issue discussions. The commit classification for PQC algorithms reveals that 90% of commits concern maintenance of existing support. From the issue discussions, we construct an 11-category taxonomy of recurring technical challenges. Build, packaging, and dependency failures, along with functional defects, account for approximately half of categorized issues. To examine how PQC support evolves, we use time-series analysis and first implementations of individual algorithms within repositories around NIST standardization milestones. After the 2024 finalization, standardized algorithm names appeared in more than 80% of the PQC development changes analyzed, although earlier names such as Kyber continued to appear. Development activity increased over the observation period. Our milestone analysis, however, did not find a significant increase in first implementations. Migration plans should therefore account for sustained maintenance, prioritize build reliability and integration testing, and track both standardized and predecessor algorithm names. We make the dataset, taxonomy, annotations, and analysis pipeline publicly available.
items.title: Understanding Post-Quantum Cryptography Adoption: Practices, Challenges, and Evolution in Open-Source Software

items.summary: Authentic records can support unauthorized narratives when their qualifications, query scope, or counterevidence are silently dropped. We present revision-bound evidence cuts, a framework for authenticating both supporting and opposing inference obligations across changing source versions. Signed complete-update frontiers permit transport of unaffected certificates, alternative-cut recovery, and an exact certified-reuse radius given by a frontier-hypergraph transversal number. Their source obligations induce an integral model of context-bound authorization. To secure database-derived claims, we introduce an authenticated relational query contract that binds original source records, complete selected bags, counting units, parameters, and aggregates independently of execution strategy. A full-source verifier checks 16,824 Chogha Mish records across SQLite scans, indexes, and materialized views; three valid strategies agree and eight contract/view mutations are rejected. A separate 340-row NISP cohort shows that changing the admitted weighting rule can reverse a comparison while preserving every source record. A frozen English text-to-frame compiler produces qualified evidence receipts, with linguistic accuracy evaluated separately from cryptographic integrity. We also separate logical-source from transport commitments so lossless re-encoding need not invalidate unchanged scientific evidence. The SCENE prototype evaluates signed revisions, authenticated queries, scoped disclosures, and adversarial mutations at scales reaching one million source records. These guarantees rely on declared policies and independently pinned trust roots; they authenticate specified computations and obligations, not historical truth, complete counterevidence, or institutional endorsement.
items.title: Revision-Bound Evidence Cuts: Authenticated Queries and Contextual Witness Capacity

items.summary: AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery (AIG-NCII) is an increasingly prevalent form of online abuse, distinguished from AI-generated sexual content (AIG-SC) by the sexualized depiction of a real person's identity without their consent. To understand how offenders may benefit from the tools and resources shared across the broader AIG-SC community, we analyzed 139 R+ guides on CivitAI, a popular platform known to host a disproportionate amount of AIG-SC. We find that AIG-SC guides discuss how to create content generation workflows composed of sexual and identity concepts, the building blocks of AIG-NCII, including one guide that explicitly outlines an AIG-NCII workflow. We identify that ultimately AIG-NCII is enabled by configuration rather than a distinct set of technical tools. We map AIG-NCII threat models across basic and advanced AIG-SC workflows to demonstrate how multiple dual-use technical components can compose NCII outputs in an environment with little to no discussion of ethical implications or responsible use. We conclude by noting that, as most workflows rely on open-weight models, existing technical defenses against AIG-NCII are limited. However, our findings offer a starting point for evaluation of AI-based models and products against realistic attacker behavior required by new EU regulation and suggest that efforts to develop safeguards at the model- and product-levels should focus on generation of identity content.
items.title: AI-Generated Non-Consensual Intimate Imagery is Configured, Not Built: How General-Purpose AI Technology Enables Sexual Violence

items.summary: An agent skill packages natural-language instructions, scripts, and reference files that an LLM-based agent loads for a task. Skills may access the file system, shell, and network under user-authorized permissions; weaknesses can lead to unsafe execution. Existing scanners primarily target malicious skills, not unintended vulnerabilities in public repositories, and analyze skills in isolation, overlooking multi-skill interactions. To address these gaps, we developed a six-module scanner: Content Extraction, Local Analysis, Composite Analysis, Validation, Reporting, and Mitigation. Local Analysis detects unintended vulnerabilities in benign skills. On a 556-case leaderboard subset of SkillTrustBench, it achieved 95.90% recall with a 4.22% false positive rate; on a balanced sample of 1,000 MalSkillBench skills, its F1 was 0.947, outperforming Cisco's Skill Scanner, NVIDIA's SkillSpector, AgentSkillsScanner, and SkillSieve. In 1,587 skills from the 75 most-starred GitHub repositories, three analysts confirmed 53 of 59 findings (89.8% precision) across 23 repositories. We developed proof-of-concept (PoC) attacks for each vulnerability, disclosed 10 medium- and high-severity cases to maintainers, and tested mitigations on the remaining cases. Composite Analysis models dependencies among skills through shared resources, invocations, and instruction-mediated interactions. On SCR-Bench, its F1 score was 0.991 (98.7% precision, 99.6% recall), versus 0.816-0.858 for three SkillsGuard configurations released with CompoSkill. It identified two composite findings on GitHub, validated by PoC attacks. The Mitigation module recommends skill substitution, patches, and configuration changes. For 47 of 55 GitHub findings, mitigations prevented PoC attacks in all trials while preserving tested legitimate functionality.
items.title: Scan Before You Install: Detecting and Mitigating Local and Composite Vulnerabilities in Skills

items.summary: Public exploit code for a newly disclosed vulnerability usually appears before any published rule that detects its exploitation. Of the 45 CVEs we evaluate, 37 ever received a Sigma, Elastic or Splunk rule; in 33 the exploit came first, by a median of 22 days. Analysts still write every rule by hand. We present Encore, which compiles a public Python proof-of-concept exploit (PoC) into CVE-specific hunting rules over a web service's existing logs, without running it. Encore rests on the PoC Behavior Alignment Principle: a PoC performs the exploit, so its code already provides a rule's HTTP requests, payloads and host operations. That is hard to act on: a PoC is written against libraries and runs on the attacker's machine, while the target's web-server, proxy and host logs record only what arrived and what it did. Encore closes the gap with a map from library calls to the operations they cause, built once per library, keeping only the operations visible on the target. For 12 of the 45, Encore's rule states the exploit's own payload fragment or host operation, which is evidence of the exploit itself, and not of traffic to its endpoint. On matched controls it separates that exploit from the same request with a harmless value, and it raises no alerts across 27,081 legitimate and crawl requests. We never compile the exploit that produced the logs. Most are Splunk's public attack data, recorded by a third party. Without reading a single log, Encore's rules find 43 of the 45. Splunk's log-tested rules cover 30 of the 45, and Encore finds 28 of those, plus all 10 CVEs without an ESCU rule. Where Splunk's rules alert on 20 wrong CVE pairs, Encore's alert on only 2. Hunting can start as soon as a PoC is public, and rules can raise an alert when it provides a payload or host operation.
items.title: Set an Exploit to Catch an Exploit: Compiling Public Proofs of Concept into Threat Hunting Rules

items.summary: Recent benchmarks show that LLMs achieve strong performance in both function-level binary understanding and end-to-end binary reverse engineering tasks, but whether LLMs can reason over interprocedural semantics in compiled binaries remains unclear. Function-level benchmarks offer limited visibility into cross-function relationships, while whole-program benchmarks typically evaluate final outcomes of tasks that may be solvable from local clues alone, making it difficult to disentangle interprocedural reasoning from exploration, tool use, execution, and retrieval. To address this limitation, we introduce ICALL-BENCH, a benchmark that directly evaluates whether LLMs and agents can understand and reason over interprocedural semantics in binary programs, using indirect-call target recovery as a measurable probe. ICALL-BENCH covers 50 complete real-world C/C++ programs spanning different complexity levels and multiple optimization configurations, with an average of 74,746 lines of code and 941 functions per program. We further introduce three analysis regimes spanning model-only reasoning, static tool-augmented agents, and Internet-enabled open-world agents to examine how intrinsic reasoning, active information acquisition, and external knowledge each contribute to interprocedural binary analysis. We evaluate five recent LLMs and their corresponding agents. Our results reveal a wide separation across current models and agents, with program-level verifiable success rates ranging from 23% to 81%. They also show that greater information access does not consistently lead to better results, with particularly limited gains on the hardest cases, where deeper interprocedural reasoning remains the primary bottleneck. Uneven performance across models and frequent verifiable failures even under an optimistic evaluation indicate that robust binary interprocedural reasoning remains an open challenge.
items.title: ICALL-BENCH: Benchmarking LLM Interprocedural Reasoning in Binary Programs

items.summary: AI compiler and runtime stacks must preserve bindings between tensor values and their operations, storage, and execution state. These bindings can fail while the underlying objects remain present, with symptoms appearing in another layer. We present TensorBound, an empirical study of tensor binding failures in IREE and the XLA and PyTorch ecosystems. The study analyzes 264 reports and reconstructs 149 distinct repaired causes through source tracing and comparisons of pre-fix and repaired revisions. Each reconstruction connects the first invalid decision to its violated condition, physical effect, and repair. Missing eligibility checks, incorrect mappings or translations, and lost or omitted relations account for 69.1% of repaired causes. These patterns highlight the need to preserve binding facts and check the conditions for their use. The 101 first invalid decisions in compiler code identify candidate checking points before execution. Four archived IREE diagnostic attempts distinguish effect localization from source-based cause explanation. Together, these findings motivate transition-specific checks that preserve binding facts across representations and enforce the required conditions at consuming decisions.
items.title: TensorBound: Characterizing Tensor Binding Failures in AI Compiler and Runtime Stacks

items.summary: Software vulnerability detection remains difficult because existing approaches rely on predefined analysis rules, learn vulnerability patterns implicitly from code and labels, or use large language models (LLMs) to make the final security judgment. It remains unclear whether structured descriptions of security-relevant program behavior can improve supervised detection. We present VulnLens, an explanation-augmented framework for binary C/C++ vulnerability detection that separates program-behavior analysis from the final decision. A label-blind LLM-based Explainer examines each function from seven fixed perspectives: data flow, memory access, object lifetime, arithmetic and type behavior, control flow, shared state, and external-resource access. Without receiving vulnerability labels or CWE information, it generates structured explanations. A supervised Detector combines source code and explanations through sequential cross-attention. We evaluate VulnLens on a PrimeVul-derived dataset covering ten CWE categories and test transfer to SecVulEval without retraining. On the 526-function PrimeVul test set, VulnLens achieves 75.5% accuracy and 77.2% F1, exceeding DeepSeek V4 Pro by 4.2 percentage points in accuracy and Gemini 2.5 Pro by 2.2 points in F1. Matched explanations improve F1 by 7.3 points over a separately trained code-only detector. On SecVulEval, VulnLens achieves 66.4% accuracy and 65.8% F1, outperforming DeepSeek V4 Pro by 7.6 points in accuracy and 20.0 points in F1, and Gemini 2.5 Pro by 16.6 points in accuracy and 7.8 points in F1.
items.title: Structured Security Explanations for Learning-Based Vulnerability Detection

items.summary: We introduce Heads of Security (HoS), a prompt injection defense that enforces instruction-data separation via a small set of learned per-head attention gates. HoS learns how each head should redistribute attention between trusted and untrusted tokens, enabling models to reason over untrusted content without following injected instructions. We evaluate HoS on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and GPT-OSS-20B. We compare it against SecAlign++, a state-of-the-art finetuning-based defense, and ASIDE, a defense that, like ours, builds instruction-data separation into the model architecture. We show that HoS offers greater robustness to adaptive attacks, better performance on standard utility benchmarks, and matches top performance on standard agentic prompt injection benchmarks. More specifically, the black-box RL-Hammer attack reaches 97% ASR against GPT-OSS-20B and 85% against SecAlign, but only 10% against HoS. Claudini, a state-of-the-art white-box attack, strengthened against HoS through autoresearch, requires 3 times more FLOPs to reach the same ASR on HoS as it does on GPT-OSS-20B or SecAlign. HoS preserves base-model utility across standard multiple-choice benchmarks and prompting setups, whereas SecAlign and ASIDE degrade in few-shot settings. On agentic benchmarks with static attacks, HoS and SecAlign perform similarly and substantially improve the security-utility trade-off over the base model. ASIDE struggles with tool use, achieving only 10% utility. These results show that prompt injection robustness can be achieved and improved through targeted attention interventions.
items.title: Heads of Security: Learned Attention Gates Improve Prompt Injection Robustness

items.summary: It is not known whether a classical polynomial-time verifier can verify arbitrary polynomial-time quantum computations with an efficient quantum honest prover without computational assumptions. We show that, relative to a classical oracle, such verification is possible for a language beyond the polynomial hierarchy that is decided exactly in quantum polynomial time. The protocol is public-coin, with perfect completeness and soundness error at most 1/4. To our knowledge, no language with such a proof system was previously proved to lie outside AM relative to an oracle. For every unbounded polynomial-time computable function, the oracle can be chosen so that the message count and the oracle query counts of the quantum algorithm, verifier, and honest prover are bounded by this function of the input length. The message count is optimal up to a constant factor, since for a suitable oracle every interactive proof system for the language uses at least a constant fraction of the messages of our protocol on infinitely many lengths, with a constant depending on its verifier. The language is a variant of recursive Fourier sampling in which code tables encode secrets that address data tables. The tables are evaluated recursively, and the oracle stores only the leaves. The quantum algorithm recovers every secret exactly, and the verifier checks the prover's secrets recursively against random code entries. The recursion restricts the input in a correlated way, as the same secret fixes the code bits and chooses the free coordinate, so Håstad's switching lemma does not apply. We prove a switching theorem for these restrictions, which may be of independent interest. For instances of sufficient height, no constant-depth circuit of size $2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}$ changes its output with probability above $2^{-Ω(n)}$ when the answer of a random instance is flipped by changing a single leaf.
items.title: Classical Verification of Quantum Computation Beyond the Polynomial Hierarchy

items.summary: Large language models are pretrained on vast, uncurated corpora scraped from the public web. This creates a security risk from attackers who plant poisoned content in the pretraining data. We show for the first time that such poisoning can plant a remote code execution backdoor in an agent, causing it to execute attacker-chosen commands on the user's machine. To measure the threat end to end, we pretrain Qwen3 models from scratch at sizes 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B, and then post-train each into a CLI agent using a clean pipeline. Poisoning only 0.1% of the pretraining corpus with our new poison design implants the backdoor: the deployed agent executes the malicious command when the trigger is present while behaving normally on clean inputs. The attack success rate (ASR) increases with model scale, with the 4B model reaching roughly 92% ASR at a 0.1% poison rate and staying positive even when the poisoning rate drops to 0.0005%. Our code is available at https://github.com/safety-research/agentic-backdoor.
items.title: Agentic Backdoors via Pretraining Poisoning

items.summary: Model quantization has become a fundamental technique for enabling the efficient deployment of large-scale deep neural networks (DNNs) in data-intensive applications by reducing model size. Despite its widespread adoption, the impact of quantization on training data privacy --- particularly vulnerability to membership inference attacks (MIAs) --- remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we present the first comprehensive empirical study of privacy risks in quantized DNNs, evaluating eight state-of-the-art MIA attacks across six representative quantization methods. Our results reveal that practical quantization levels (4-8 bits) have limited impact on membership privacy risks, with quantized models remaining largely as vulnerable as their full-precision counterparts. Although aggressive low-bit quantization (e.g., 2-bit) can provide meaningful privacy gains, these benefits come at the cost of substantial utility degradation. To understand the underlying causes of these observations, we systematically analyze how different quantization strategies affect model behaviors and outputs, and how these changes influence privacy vulnerability. Beyond evaluating attack risks, we further investigate whether existing privacy defenses developed for full-precision DNNs can effectively protect QNNs. Our results show that these defenses provide only limited additional privacy protection when applied to quantized models, while further amplifying utility degradation. Our study provides practical guidance for privacy-aware deployment of quantized DNNs and motivates the development of new attack and defense mechanisms for QNNs. Our code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/JeffffffFu/Priv-QDNN.
items.title: Revisiting Privacy Risks in Quantized Deep Neural Networks

items.summary: HTTP method semantics are a common boundary between safe retrieval and state-changing operations; however, deployed web applications do not always enforce this boundary consistently. In this paper, we study HTTP method interchangeability, a behavior where a POST request can be rewritten as a GET request to the same endpoint, with POST body parameters moved into the query string, while preserving an equivalent observed response. We present Method Interchange Detection Engine (MIDE), an automated pipeline that crawls web applications in a browser, records POST requests generated by page loads and user-interface interactions, converts supported POST bodies into GET candidates, and compares replayed responses with the original POST response. To avoid counting generic or parameter-independent responses as interchangeable, MIDE also sends a no-query GET baseline. We treat as high-confidence evidence of interchangeability only the cases where the converted GET matches the POST, while the baseline does not. We perform a large-scale unauthenticated experiment on the Tranco top 10k. We find high-confidence interchangeable requests on 407 of 10,000 tested sites (4.1%), 407 of 3,200 sites with captured POSTs (12.7%), and 407 of 2,734 sites with replayed POSTs (14.9%). A targeted Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) token-replay check finds cases where invalid tokens are rejected for POST but accepted for the equivalent GET. We also observe Web Cache Deception (WCD) conditions and cacheable GET responses for interchangeable request instances. These results demonstrate that method interchangeability is observable in real web applications and can expose method-scoped defense gaps.
items.title: When POST Becomes GET: Investigating HTTP Method Interchangeability and Its Security Implications

items.summary: AI chatbot platforms have become one of the most popular web interfaces users interact with online, routinely receiving personal and intimate information shared under an expectation of privacy. Yet, on the web application side, these platforms have the ability to embed third-party analytics, advertising, and session replay scripts that operate silently alongside the chatbot, creating an underexamined channel for conversational data leakage towards third parties. We conduct the first systematic large-scale measurement study of contextual leakage in AI chatbots, auditing the web interfaces of 42 general-purpose and domain-specific (health, legal, and education) platforms. Beyond standard network interception, we instrument the browser at the JavaScript engine level to attribute each data flow to the exact user action that triggered it, and the DOM capture mechanism used to retrieve its content, a granularity invisible to network-layer analysis alone. We find that 21 of these platforms leak conversation titles to third-party trackers, while nine leak verbatim user prompts. Beyond content, we observe a substantial amount of chatbot platforms sending user emails to third-party trackers, enabling the association of conversational context with a user's identity. Our findings cast traditional web privacy issues under a new light, highlighting the privacy issues that are inherent in how users interact with modern AI chatbots.
items.title: Penny for Your Prompts: A Measurement Study of Contextual Leakage in AI Chat Platforms

items.summary: Data memory-dependent prefetchers (DMPs) are a microarchitectural optimization recently introduced in mainstream desktop and server CPUs. Although DMPs offer performance improvements, they have been shown to enable side-channel leakage of secrets, even from constant-time code that has been hardened against Spectre attacks. Unfortunately, existing defenses either incur significant performance overhead or, as we show, fail to prevent all DMP leakage. In this work, we address this gap by designing a defense that is both secure and efficient. First, we propose a classification of DMP leakage, categorize existing and novel attacks, and analyze which leakage classes are mitigated by existing defenses. We validate this analysis empirically by implementing the first open-source DMPs on a RISC-V processor, showing that the only existing defense that aims to preserve DMP performance fails to protect against entire leakage classes. Next, we propose SecDMP, a provably secure and efficient hardware-based defense. SecDMP requires secrets to be marked in memory and ensures that DMPs never encode these secrets in the microarchitecture---without compromising performance for public data. We formally prove that SecDMP introduces no leakage beyond a baseline semantics without DMPs. Notably, when combined with speculative-execution defenses, SecDMP restores complete microarchitectural security for constant-time code. Finally, our empirical evaluation shows that SecDMP prevents all DMP leakage while incurring minimal performance overhead and hardware cost.
items.title: SecDMP: Provably Secure Data Memory-Dependent Prefetching (Extended Version)

items.summary: Prior work framed the envelope layer as the channel through which malicious content enters an agent, and established it as a defense surface independent of the LLM layer and the agent layer; however, that work only tested the envelope layer briefly and did not examine how label strength, envelope authenticity, scaffold differences, or existing memories affect defense effectiveness. Following its GDA Measurement methodology and the A/B/C/D outcome taxonomy, this paper takes the A2A-TIBA attack as the test vehicle, uses the semantic breach rate as the primary indicator with the semantic refusal rate as its complementary reference, and characterizes the security boundary of the envelope layer through a two-by-two factorial experiment and a memory experiment. The results show that: when the envelope is authentic, strong labels consistently reduce the semantic breach rate, whereas weak labels are not necessarily better than an unlabeled baseline; when the envelope can be forged, the benefit of strong labels is weakened and its direction varies across frontends; and memory has a larger effect than any label manipulation: success memory raises the semantic breach rate while failure memory lowers it, and most combinations that contain both experiences return to the no-memory baseline. Accordingly, this paper refines the envelope layer from a single admission channel into two levels, an admission channel plus a context assembly surface, and argues that its security boundary is not a fixed property of labels but a dynamic outcome jointly shaped by label claims, frontend permissions, and historical memory.
items.title: The Envelope Layer: An Underestimated Surface of LLM Agent Defense

items.summary: Modern agent frameworks allow users to provide Markdown files containing system prompts, tool descriptions, and skill definitions (e.g., SKILL.md), which are incorporated into the agent's context during initialization. In this work, we investigate whether this configuration mechanism can also serve as an injection channel: can a jailbreak embedded in a Markdown skill file propagate through an agent and induce prohibited behavior? To answer this question, we construct a LangChain-based question-answering agent whose system prompt is assembled from a user-provided Markdown file. We embed a jailbreak combining persona manipulation with a GPTFUZZER-based attack and evaluate its effectiveness across seven contemporary open-weight models using 270 forbidden questions spanning nine harm categories. Under a benign system prompt, the models exhibit near-complete refusal behavior, with a mean attack success rate (ASR) of just 0.5%. In contrast, the injected skill file raises the mean ASR to 45%, reaching 68.9% for individual models. We further evaluate two payload obfuscation strategies: an invisible zero-width character-based stealth payload and a phonetic payload based on grapheme-to-phoneme transformations. Neither outperforms the plain-text injection; notably, the phonetic variant reduces mean ASR to 30%. These findings identify Markdown skill files as an underexplored attack surface for AI agents and suggest that vulnerability to configuration-based jailbreaks depends more strongly on the underlying model than on the specific payload obfuscation technique.
items.title: Poisoned Skills: Propagating Jailbreaks Through Agent Markdown Files

items.summary: Agentic Entity Resolution (ER) systems iteratively plan actions, retrieve evidence, revise hypotheses, and propose graph mutations. An erroneous identity hypothesis may condition later retrieval and produce apparent confirmation. This paper proposes a Digital Identity Optimization (DIO) and Ontology of Digital Identity (ODI)-informed authorization boundary between evidence available for agent reasoning and evidence eligible to authorize persistent identity-changing mutations. A domain-governed constraint-binding function maps selected reconstruction-failure distinctions to explicit identity-preserving constraints. An abstract two-phase supervisor permits a commit only when claim-specific authorization-eligible evidence supports every required proposition, relevant conflicts are resolved, the operation remains within its authorized scope, and relevant state and policy versions remain valid. Admission as UNVERIFIED does not confer authorization eligibility. Separate claim-specific promotion governs evidentiary use; insufficient support or unresolved material conflict leads to deferral. The contribution is a specification connecting diagnostic-to-constraint mapping, evidence promotion, proposition coverage, conflict handling, scope binding, and commit-time version integrity. A proposed evaluation protocol is designed to assess the mapping's incremental value beyond generic authorization and conventional identifier rules. This is a conceptual architecture without implementation or empirical validation, not a theorem of semantic correctness. Its property depends on domain-policy adequacy, evidence promotion, and enforcement. It does not prevent erroneous hypotheses or hypothesis-conditioned retrieval; dependency-aware evidence flow remains future research.
items.title: Constraining the Commit Boundary: A DIO/ODI-Informed Authorization Guardrail for Agentic Entity Resolution

items.summary: Proprietary language models and their reasoning traces are vulnerable to API-based distillation, where an adversary trains a student model on the teacher model's outputs. To obtain evidence of distillation, model providers can watermark the teacher's outputs, aiming to leave a radioactive signal in the student's outputs. Existing black-box detectors search for such radioactivity using token-level statistics of the suspect model's outputs. However, token-level signals are not always detectable, for instance when the distillation traces are sampled at a low temperature. In this work, we discover the watermark basin, a persistent signal that enables more reliable watermark detection: during fine-tuning, watermarked teacher traces embed a distinct, key-specific geometric signal in parameter space that lies orthogonal to the ordinary task-specific fine-tuning subspace. Building on this, we introduce Watermark Basin Alignment (WM-Basin), a black-box watermark detector that queries the suspect model through its API, without access to its weights or logits. WM-Basin maps generated text to gradient representations using a fixed clean probe model, projects out the ordinary fine-tuning task directions, and tests whether the residual gradient aligns with the watermark basin induced by the watermark key. We evaluate WM-Basin extensively across diverse teacher models and student architectures (from 135M to 8.2B parameters) distilled on mathematical reasoning. At a strict 0.1% false-positive rate, WM-Basin detects 79% of distilled models at n-gram=1 and 45% at n-gram=3, substantially improving over the state-of-the-art token-level baseline (29% and 1.3%, respectively). Because the watermark signal resides in a persistent basin, it survives post-distillation modifications including quantization, pruning, and reinforcement-learning post-training.
items.title: Watermark Basins: Black-Box Detection of Distilled LLMs

items.summary: Multi-relational graph detectors learn from clean data how much to trust each relation, but an adversary pays a different price to manipulate each relation and each action; taking such costs as given, we ask when using a relation is worse than ignoring it. Our first main result proves that degree gating strictly beats every selection or reweighting of a relation when part of the population is isolated on it and the attacker cannot afford to open the gate, and that this window is sharp; on real graphs, validated gating gains exactly on the relations that meet these conditions and nowhere else. Our second shows that a per-node exposure bound, which extends to message passing, tells a platform which relation to harden: exposure per unit cost, computed without any attack, picks the relation whose hardening raises the exact trap threshold most in 15 of 16 cases, against at most 7 for informativeness, cheapness, or an analysis with equal edit costs. Supporting tools give exact worst cases for linear relational models, certified brackets for R-GCN and tree ensembles, and a finite-sample guarantee for adversarial validation, under which clean-trained graph detectors fall below their graph-free counterparts in 58 of 90 settings on six graphs. A selection protocol built on these results is never significantly worse than ignoring the graph; with at most four relations it mostly abstains, as validation alone would, and its cost-aware proposals help when relations are many, so far shown on synthetic graphs. Without cost information, the safe choice is to abstain.
items.title: When Is a Relation Worth Trusting? Manipulation Costs, Exposure, and the Trust Trap in Multi-Relational Graph Learning

items.summary: Modern secret sharing protocols promise robust secret sharing in fully asynchronous Byzantine systems, but their practical costs remain difficult to compare across papers, assumptions, and workloads. The difficulty is not merely experimental: protocols with similar asymptotic guarantees often place very different work on the critical path through their choices of dissemination, verification, batching, and recovery. This paper turns that fragmented research landscape into a corpus-backed designspace analysis and systems evaluation of asynchronous verifiable and complete secret sharing. We derive a design sieve, select seven representative protocols, and implement them in a common Rust framework. In our experiments on the Grid'5000 platform, we evaluate honest-dealer and faulty-dealer stress executions using latency, throughput, message count, bandwidth, and aggregate CPU-time. The results show that message complexity alone poorly predicts latency, that optimistic paths can be dominated by recovery cost, and that batching or packing helps only when verification stays off the critical path. These findings turn protocol-by-protocol comparisons into design-to-cost guidance for choosing, implementing, and extending asynchronous verifiable and complete sharing protocols.
items.title: Asynchronous Verifiable and Complete Secret Sharing: From Design Patterns to System-Level Trade-offs

items.summary: Agent skills, reusable instruction packages centred on a SKILL.md file, extend AI agents on demand, and a single line in a widely copied skill reaches every agent that loads it. Some lines are oversight-loosening directives: they tell the agent to proceed without approval, to bypass checks with --no-verify, or to keep working without checking in. Although such directives can remove a checkpoint from every agent that loads them, no prior work has examined them. We present the first large-scale study of oversight-loosening directives, analyzing 1.53 million English skills from GitSkills. We split skills into units (sentences, bullets, table cells, and code lines), develop a codebook that labels oversight directives by polarity, mechanism, and scope, label 2,097 units by hand, and train a detector to scale the analysis. Our results show that about one in seventeen skills (about 88,000 skills) contains a loosening directive. These directives most often loosen oversight through permission flags, and most of them (70.1%) apply unconditionally rather than only in specific contexts such as CI. Compared with skills that have the same amount of oversight language, skills that run shell code, install packages, or use sudo have 1.7-1.8 times the odds of containing a loosening directive, an association that holds across all our robustness checks, and they do not compensate with more tightening. Loosening spreads through a few upstream skills rather than through edits by their adopters: 2.4% of the skill families that carry loosening account for half of all copies of loosening-carrying skills, and 1.1% of distinct loosening units for half of all loosening occurrences. Open-source skill scanners catch at most 46% of loosening directives, with a precision below 0.4, while the LLM behind them, prompted with our codebook instead, catches 61% at a precision of 0.71.
items.title: When Skills Tell Agents Not to Ask: A Large-Scale Study of Oversight Directives in Agent Skills

items.summary: All traditional encryption schemes share a fundamental operational vulnerability: encrypted data must be decrypted before it can be used. Fully homomorphic encryption eliminates this vulnerability by enabling computation directly on encrypted data, but existing FHE schemes impose substantial practical constraints that limit deployment. This paper presents a formal security analysis of the Gribov-Kahrobaei-Shpilrain (GKS) private-key FHE scheme. GKS requires no bootstrapping or de-linearization, produces bit-exact decryption, supports native encrypted search, and scales to unbounded depth.
items.title: GKS Fully Homomorphic Encryption: Security Analysis

items.summary: Automotive cybersecurity commonly assumes benign end-product manufacturers and design authorities, focusing on supply-chain threats, external attacks, and compromised network participants observable through misbehaviour. This assumption overlooks malicious-by-design vehicles that remain authentic and protocol-conformant while performing undeclared sensing, communication, or context-triggered actuation. We formulate an Entity-Centric Threat Model spanning three subcomponents. The first, Malign Entity Archetypes, describes four types of malign entity: peer-benign, purpose-malicious vehicles; compromised vehicles; reappropriated genuine components; and imitated vehicles or components. The model exposes two assurance gaps: authenticity does not establish declared-purpose conformance, while malicious functionality can evade detection based on behavioural history or peer-visible evidence. Reappropriated components can remain genuine and retain usable identities or capabilities outside authorised contexts, reducing the effectiveness of signal fingerprinting and certificate-based authentication. To structure this threat space, we introduce a Behaviour-Locus Matrix that maps covert, overt, and concealment actions across hardware, software, and network loci. For peer-benign, purpose-malicious vehicles, we further present a Behavioural Interaction Model that represents how hidden capabilities are contextually activated, realised through actions, manifested within the vehicle and its environment, and potentially observed or concealed.
items.title: Janus Vehicles: Entity-Centric Threat Modelling of Protocol-Conformant Vehicles under a Malicious-Manufacturer Assumption

items.summary: Audit-based certification bounds the violation rate of an LLM agent by auditing a random fraction $\varepsilon$ of actions and reweighting the audited labels; its validity is meant to rest only on the defender's audit coin. We show that it also rests on a confidentiality property: the coin must not interfere with the agent's view before the action commits, at a time the agent chooses. We call this pre-commit noninterference (PNI) and measure its violation by $D_{\mathrm{A}}$, the total-variation distance between the agent's views under the two coin values. PNI is necessary and sufficient for an unbiased certificate against adaptive agents, the worst-case bias is $(1-\varepsilon)D_{\mathrm{A}}$, and no procedure that sees only audited labels can pay less. Leakage composes across steps, a resource shared across episodes opens a channel of computable size, and raising the audit rate cannot restore validity. On a monitor we built, a silent audit changes no output but adds latency that tool timestamps expose, and the agent can enlarge it. A real LLM agent follows an injection that names a visible audit notice (generic, tool, and timing clauses have no effect); over that channel the plain certificate fails on measured labels and, by a post-hoc analysis, in a live run on a pre-registered schedule, while a silent audit restores it. A fresh coin per audited call closes the timing channel; padding only narrows it.
items.title: Blindfold: Keeping the Audit Coin Secret from LLM Agents

items.summary: Despite significant advances in computer vision, semantic segmentation models remain vulnerable to backdoor attacks, posing a security risk. These attacks redirect pixels of a chosen victim class to an attacker-specified target class when a trigger is present, while preserving clean predictions. Existing defenses are largely derived from image classification, while dedicated segmentation defenses remain scarce and typically require retraining or model modification. We introduce RePAIR, a post-hoc, label-free, attack-unaware defense based on the observation that backdoor-induced shifts can be stronger in the classifier head than in internal representations, leaving recoverable victim-class semantics. RePAIR infers the victim-target relation from an unlabeled, potentially contaminated image pool, constructs a safety-approved semantic reference, and localizes suspicious pixels by comparing head predictions with internal semantic evidence. It then applies feature-space and output corrections toward the inferred victim semantics, while conservative localization and output constraints limit changes to benign predictions. We model the attack as adversarial probability transport and repair as its approximate reversal, deriving bounds and sufficient conditions for localization, residual attack success, clean-side changes, defense-induced target predictions, and attack-unaware pair identification. Experiments across segmentation architectures and attack settings show that RePAIR substantially reduces attack success while largely preserving clean performance.
items.title: RePAIR: Inverting Backdoor Attacks in Semantic Segmentation

items.summary: Modern image generators can produce complex visual artifacts, including diagrams, interfaces, and records that combine text, graphics, and layout to convey detailed information. They may refuse requests for overtly harmful imagery yet still generate artifacts that guide dangerous actions or support deception. We call the risk arising from what such images enable, rather than only what they depict, functional visual harm (FVH). Existing safety benchmarks focus largely on overtly harmful content, such as pornography and graphic violence, leaving image generators' safety alignment against FVH insufficiently evaluated. To address this gap, we introduce FVH-Bench, comprising 669 prompts across five harmful visual functions and ten risk domains. The 11 evaluated image generators rarely refuse these requests and frequently generate artifacts that fulfill the targeted harmful functions. High scores for target harm realization and harmful artifact usability further indicate that these outputs can support the intended harmful purposes. A further analysis finds that existing safety detectors also provide limited coverage of FVH, indicating gaps in their ability to recognize harmful visual functions. Together, these findings show that evaluating image-generator safety alignment requires considering not only what images depict, but also what they may enable.
items.title: FVH-Bench: Evaluating Image Generator Safety Beyond Overtly Harmful Imagery

items.summary: Log messages are employed to identify anomalies in IoT systems and have been widely used across many applications. To enable collaboration among infrastructures belonging to different organizations, federated log anomaly detection has been thoroughly investigated for this purpose, often assuming the availability of ground truth log templates. However, this is typically not the case, as it is still necessary to depend on log parsers to extract log templates at inference time, while the design and deployment of such parsers in distributed environments remains largely an open problem. To this end, we report on an empirical investigation of distributed parsing and its key challenges, providing insights and lessons learned towards closing the gap between research and application. To further refine and contextualize the resulting benchmarks, we examine and introduce new metrics that provide a more comprehensive view for evaluating distributed parsers and how they behave in distributed environments. We propose a set of lessons learned and recommendations to support the design, deployment, and evaluation of distributed parsers. In particular, we evaluate the performance of five distinct parsing algorithms in combination with aggregation techniques that allow a unified agreement of event-template mappings across all participating clients, a prerequisite for federated log anomaly detection. In total, 6,720 distinct distributed configurations were tested for this purpose.
items.title: Too many clients spoil the logs: distributed parsing, aggregation techniques and metrics

items.summary: As smart organizations increasingly rely on technologies like AI, big data, and IoT, securing these systems is crucial. This research introduces a dynamic multi-factor authentication (MFA) system within the Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA) framework, which enforces continuous verification. The system randomly selects biometric authentication factors, such as fingerprint, iris, and face recognition using a Markov chain model to ensure adaptability and reduce predictability in security measures. Using CASIA biometric datasets and AES-128 encryption, the system securely manages user data and authentication. Performance analysis shows that the dynamic selection process balances security and efficiency, making it suitable for smart organizations, particularly in e-government contexts. This MFA system strengthens cybersecurity by providing a flexible, real-time defense against evolving threats.
items.title: Developing a Dynamic Multi-factor Authentication System for Securing Smart Organizations

items.summary: Payment channel hubs (PCHs) enable private cross-chain payments, but existing protocols remain difficult to extend across heterogeneous blockchains. Their payment flows often depend on how particular blockchains represent transactions, authorize channel updates, and settle balances. Some protocols do not explain how their channels are implemented on actual blockchains. Supporting a new ledger or execution model requires a corresponding channel realization and may also require protocol adaptation and security analysis. We present UniPCH, a framework with two layers that separates native channel execution from private cross-chain payment logic. The lower UniPC layer defines common state transitions and security requirements. It separates task authorization from confirmation of the complete channel state. We provide realizations for UTXO ledgers and account ledgers that support smart contracts. At the upper layer, we develop selective re-signing blind conditional signatures (S-RBCS) to coordinate conditional authorization across hubs. Using S-RBCS, we construct a payment protocol that coordinates different channels in four phases. Our analysis establishes local UniPC security, griefing resistance, economic atomicity, and session unlinkability. We implement a Go prototype and evaluate the running time and bandwidth of each phase under different network conditions and system parameters. Results show modest computational overhead from the common interfaces. Most evaluated configurations run faster than comparable schemes under network delay. A full refresh ablation shows that reusing valid task evidence reduces computation and communication costs in the account realization.
items.title: UniPCH: A Unified Framework for Cross-Chain Payments via Payment Channel Hubs
